title: These Teachers Were Charged With Sexual Abuse. California Could Have Revoked Their Licenses Earlier but Didn’t.
author: Holly McDede
content:
Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David
Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been
sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap,
rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.

But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough
investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019.
And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t
until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d
gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them,
prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had
touched him, too.  

The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the
credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing
students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency
that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with
Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new
complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by
KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent
his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who
touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his
crotch, according to court records.

In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the
students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and
attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers,
including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer
panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of
wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former
members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that
ultimately decides teacher discipline.

After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein,
superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first
accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this
monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public
records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa
Paula at the time students accused Braff.)

In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing
agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own
investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to
police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and
“vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s
credentials.

"We sent all the evidence we had gathered," Weinstein said. "The district did
everything in its legal capacity it could.”

Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13
from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not
guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura
County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined
to comment.

Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not
touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that
he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee,
according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.

“Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around;
and he would not be closer than arm's length,” the report said, summarizing
the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them
afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk
to.”

![A man in a suit and tie holds a certificate of recognition with his name,
David Braff, while posing for a photo next to three other
people.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/515500359_24235329292757593_2688718077186072169_n_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)The
Santa Paula Unified School District recognized guidance counselor David Braff
as employee of the month in 2017. The district reported him to the state for
misconduct two years later. Santa Paula Unified School District via Facebook

Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing,
said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are
convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that
“unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal
offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action
for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific
cases or details of the investigative process.

Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing
teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of
punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role
to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who
have been accused but not convicted.”

California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh
said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system,
prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”  

“We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future," she said.

### Students Not Interviewed

In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing
received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s
alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts
to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of
misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four
years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into
complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them
inappropriately.

The district told the state agency that it had contemplated but did not
initiate any discipline against Braff before accepting his resignation. The
district said it appeared, based on student interviews, that Braff “had
engaged in at least inappropriate conduct.” Its report to the state, submitted
two months after he resigned, included a 20-page summary of the principal’s
interviews with at least seven accusers and two witnesses. It also included
Braff’s defense and noted multiple inconsistencies in his account of what had
occurred.

One fifth grade girl said that during a visit to his office, Braff had locked
the door, grabbed her by her hips and forced her to sit on his lap, according
to the district’s report to the state of its investigation. She said she did
not like being touched and cried every time she had to see him for counseling.
The girl requested to transfer to another school, district investigators said,
because she wanted to “be away from” Braff.

Two other girls alleged Braff touched them near their “privates,” the district
reported to the state. Neither girl was aware of the other’s claim.

One of them, a fourth grader, told the principal that she had been meeting
regularly with Braff for counseling since second grade. During those visits,
he would make her sit on his lap. She told the principal that Braff tapped her
on the leg with his hand “in a way to try to make her feel like she was doing
a good job,” but she said the tapping hurt. After two school years of regular
counseling, she alleged he started tapping her higher on the thigh, close to
her “private.” In contrast, she said a different teacher pats students on the
head when they do a good job, according to the district’s report to the state.

The girl, who is now 18, spoke to KQED and ProPublica with her mother and
attorney present on the condition that only her first initial, J., be used to
protect her privacy. J. said Braff had told her that whatever happened in his
office was a secret. She said she had few friends at the school and was
terrified of getting in trouble when she reported the person she confided in.

![A handwritten statement reads: “When did he touch you? He touch me last year
and this year. And he’ll close his door as well. Where did he touch you? He
touch me his offices and he put hand on my leg but almost touching my pirvate
part and that not ok. On Friday he told us he was
sorry.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Braff-
letter_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)A handwritten statement
submitted by one of Braff’s student victims in 2018. Santa Paula Unified
School District

The district’s report to the state included notes from an interview with J.’s
former principal, Lydia Olivo, who had left the school before J. and other
students complained about Braff. Olivo told Santa Paula investigators that J.
was “not always honest,” the report said. Olivo described Braff as a reliable
employee who had strong relationships with parents, staff and students. She
“seemed surprised that any of this could have occurred while she had been
Principal at McKevett,” the district’s report said. Olivo did not respond to
calls, emails and texts seeking comment.

During the district’s investigation, Braff acknowledged touching students on
the knee. “He explained if someone is crying, he taps on the knee to say they
are doing a good job to get the sad feelings out,” according to the district’s
report to the state. “When asked to demonstrate, Mr. Braff showed a slap on
his own knee.”

Nonetheless, the educator licensing agency appears not to have attempted to
reconcile the very different accounts of Braff’s behavior. Informed of Olivo’s
characterization of her complaint, J. and her mother told KQED and ProPublica
that no one at the state agency had called to ask them about it or sought to
verify any details, even though the district’s report to the state included
J.’s contact information along with that of the other students.

“If a little girl comes up to you and says something, maybe you should not say
that they're a liar,” J. said.

"They should interview students themselves and not just rely on the school
district. Do a legit investigation,” said J.’s mother, who did not know that
the state had decided not to discipline Braff until the news outlets alerted
her.

Fitzhugh, the spokesperson for the teacher credentialing agency, did not
answer questions as to why J. was not interviewed or whether anyone else was.
The case was assigned to a staffer whose job description did not include
interviewing victims.

At least one other student who had reported Braff for touching her
inappropriately also told KQED and ProPublica that no one from the state
contacted her about her allegations.

A former agency investigator, who reviewed the district’s report to the state
at the request of the news outlets, said she believed the students’
accusations because the district’s investigation described multiple children
making similar claims. She also noted the contradictions in Braff’s responses.
Cases involving allegations of inappropriately touching students should always
be assigned to investigators trained to interview victims, she said.

"Any claim of sexual misconduct should go to somebody who's going to be making
phone calls,” said the investigator, who spoke on the condition of anonymity
to protect her current job. “This man is grooming these children. There's no
other way to look at it to me. Their stories are credible.”

Per state law, the agency staff assigned to look into Braff’s case did not
make recommendations about whether or how to discipline him. That
recommendation is left up to a little-known group of volunteers who meet
monthly at the agency’s Sacramento headquarters to weigh reports from state
investigators, school districts, police and others. That volunteer panel sends
its recommendations to the 19 commissioners of the credentialing body, most of
whom are appointed by the governor.

If the panel does recommend discipline, the commissioners have the final say.
However, if the panel decides that no punishment is warranted, the
commissioners do not review that case.

Two former investigators at the state agency told the news organizations that
the panel’s recommendations did not always align with the evidence they found.
"Sometimes, as investigators, we'll see the recommendations, and we'll be
like, 'What the hell happened here?’” one former investigator said.

### “I Was Consistently Shocked”

Over three days in December 2020, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic,
members of the volunteer panel, known as the Committee of Credentials, dialed
into their monthly phone meeting to address [198
cases](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28913348-2023-24-dle-annual-
report/) of educators accused of misconduct. Among them was Braff, who by then
was working in another school.

The volunteers included a retired law enforcement officer, a school board
member, a school administrator, an education consultant and several teachers.
They had been selected by the commissioners for two-year terms.

State regulations give the volunteer committee broad latitude when assessing
allegations of teacher misconduct and recommending discipline to the
commission. Unlike jurors in a criminal trial, who need to believe a case is
proven beyond a reasonable doubt in order to convict, the committee [only
needs to find “probable
cause”](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/2009/edc/44240-44248.html)
before recommending a reprimand, a far lower standard.

“It's where a normal and reasonable person would feel that there's a chance
that this person did this,” said Steve Thorpe, the former law enforcement
officer who served on the committee when Braff’s case was reviewed. “It’s a
low threshold. You know it when you see it.” He declined to comment on Braff’s
case.

The fact that Braff’s case was not forwarded to the commissioners, former
committee members said, meant the majority of the seven-member panel did not
see enough evidence in the district’s investigation and the state’s report to
discipline Braff.

One former committee member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear
of repercussions from the teacher licensing agency, said she tends to
scrutinize district investigations because administrators can misrepresent the
facts or ask children leading questions.

Another former committee member who served during the Braff case said that
they were generally alarmed to hear some fellow members dismiss children as
unreliable sources. The person, who declined to comment on Braff’s case, spoke
on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.

![Four people with laptops sit around one end of a long conference
table.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/260318-ProPublica-
CATeacherDiscipline-02-BL_qed_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)The
Committee of Credentials, a volunteer panel, met in March 2026 to review cases
involving alleged educator misconduct. A version of the committee met by
telephone in 2020 to decide on Braff’s case. Beth LaBerge/KQED

"I was consistently shocked,” they said. “To have committee members discuss
serious allegations as, 'Well, you know how girls can be. They say all kinds
of things they don't mean,' is an unacceptable, antiquated point of view. What
if we get this wrong? Who are we allowing in the classroom?”

By the time the committee decided against recommending punishment for Braff,
he had already been working as a counselor at a different elementary school in
Los Angeles for more than a year. (A former student at that charter school
would tell police after Braff’s 2024 arrest that the counselor had touched the
boy's thigh near his groin when the two met in his office, according to a
court transcript from his criminal case.)

In 2022, nearly two years after the state closed Braff’s case, a school
administrator reported to the district that one of the girls who had accused
Braff of abuse continued to suffer severe anxiety and could not be in rooms
alone with men. Another had attempted suicide multiple times and spent a year
in residential treatment, she wrote in an email obtained by KQED and
ProPublica.  

In his response, an assistant superintendent informed the administrator that
the district had previously filed with the state to have Braff’s credential
revoked or suspended but the agency chose not to do so. “At this point, I
think pursing this matter legally is the best way to address these issues,” he
wrote, referring to following up with Santa Paula police.

Santa Paula administrators did not respond to requests for comment.

### Two Additional Cases

KQED and ProPublica identified at least two other educators who, like Braff,
were reported by their school districts to the state for sexual misconduct but
were allowed to keep teaching until they were criminally charged. Each would
draw additional allegations of sexual abuse.

As in the Braff case, the volunteer committee in these two cases evaluated
much of the same evidence as police, including complaints detailing students’
experiences. And in both cases, investigators with the teacher credentialing
agency did not interview some victims.

In one, a Southern California school district shared with the state agency
screenshots of messages that middle school math teacher Brashawn Washington
had sent to his 11-year-old student, who he regularly contacted through the
video game Fortnite. Those messages included a TikTok video showing another
boy’s penis. (At his trial, Washington told jurors that he did not send the
video to his student.)

The Romoland School District also shared with the state screenshots of
Washington’s Google Hangouts chats asking the student if he worked out,
calling him “guapo,” or handsome, and sending him kissing emojis.

The boy’s mother had provided the screenshots from her son’s phone to the
school in May 2020, according to public records obtained from Romoland. The
school district promptly alerted police and began its own investigation,
filing a report to the teacher credentialing agency that summer, district
records show.

The district included in its report the mother’s contact information, records
show. But neither the student nor his mother were interviewed, the mother told
KQED and ProPublica. Fitzhugh, the credentialing agency spokesperson, did not
answer questions about how state investigators decided who, if anyone, to
interview.

A Romoland administrator who said the district shared the screenshots with the
state as part of its report did not answer questions about the state’s
response.

Washington resigned during the school’s investigation and soon got hired at
Pasadena High School starting in the fall of 2020. Washington, teaching
virtually at first during the pandemic, continued messaging students over
Fortnite despite district policy prohibiting personal contact with students.
He had been teaching there for seven months when the volunteer committee
recommended a 21-day suspension in March. (Commissioners did not approve the
suspension until after school let out.)

State law did not require Washington to notify the Pasadena school district of
the recommended suspension. Nor did the teacher licensing agency have to alert
his new employer of any discipline if it did not know where he was employed.  

Just as his suspension was set to begin in July 2021, Washington was arrested
— and the state suspended his credentials indefinitely.

![A Black man wearing a red and black buttoned shirt, red tie and black face
mask gestures at the front of a classroom.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-1314062940.jpg?w=752)Brashawn Washington
at Pasadena High School in April 2021, during his first year as a math teacher
there. He had resigned from the Romoland School District in the year prior
after a sexual misconduct investigation. Sarah Reingewirtz, Los Angeles Daily
News/SCNG

The next year, while out on bail, Washington sent a Pasadena High student
images of himself having oral sex with another man, among other messages,
according to court records. At Washington’s 2024 criminal trial, that student
testified that the teacher had also asked him to share naked pictures of
himself when he was 16. Washington told jurors that he did not know the
student was a minor. He was sentenced to eight years and eight months in
prison for [multiple sex
offenses](https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/6a202374eaa021ae7251bd1a),
including “annoying or molesting” the Romoland student by sending him the
video, as well as producing and possessing child sex abuse material related to
minors who were not his students.

A spokesperson for Pasadena Unified did not respond to questions regarding
Washington's hiring or the state’s recommended discipline, but said in a
written statement that the district conducts background checks during the
hiring process.

Both Washington and his former attorney declined to comment.

A similar pattern unfolded with a San Francisco Bay Area elementary teacher,
Matthew Shelton, who was [convicted of sexually
abusing](https://www.kqed.org/news/12105970/former-benicia-elementary-teacher-
found-guilty-of-sexually-abusing-his-students) four students last month.

Shelton had first been arrested in 2007 on charges of [sexually abusing
students in Napa Valley](https://www.kqed.org/news/12101885/a-bay-area-
teacher-was-acquitted-of-sexual-abuse-hes-on-trial-again-for-new-allegations).
Three third-graders had told police he touched their butts or crotches, or
made them touch his penis during class.

Shelton was acquitted in that case, but the state's licensing body did
investigate the claims. At the time, Shelton told state investigators that the
students had made up the allegations and that he passed a polygraph test,
which he had obtained himself. Two of those former students told KQED and
ProPublica that state investigators never interviewed them. The agency did not
respond to questions about why the students were not interviewed.

![A white man in a blue dress shirt and patterned tie walks into a courthouse.
](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260928_BeniciaTeacherTrial_GC-14_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)Matthew
Shelton was convicted of sexually abusing four students. Gina Castro/KQED

In 2008, the licensing agency issued Shelton a confidential written warning,
which was expunged after three years, according to trial testimony. That
decision meant Shelton was able to keep teaching for the long term; he had
already begun a new job in nearby Benicia.

Years later, in 2022, students began accusing Shelton of touching them
inappropriately. The Benicia school district and a student’s parents reported
him to the state commission in 2023. More students came forward and told
police that Shelton had touched their crotch or butt over their clothing; one
student said he made her touch his penis when she was in first grade during a
school field trip.

Shelton resigned but quickly got a job at another school. As with the other
cases, the new school said it had no information about the ongoing
investigation. It also had no knowledge of his earlier warning, which had been
expunged more than a decade earlier.

This time around, however, things unfolded differently: While the state did
not alert the new school about any problems, a parent did. In September, just
weeks into the school year, Shelton’s new employer learned from a Benicia
parent about the active police investigation as well as the earlier issues in
Napa.

Shelton was immediately put on leave. In February 2024, prosecutors charged
him, requiring the state licensing agency to automatically suspend his
credentials. Unlike in Napa, the agency revoked his license in July 2024
without waiting for a conviction.

Shelton did not respond to requests for comment, and his attorney declined to
comment. He is due to be sentenced in December. Benicia Superintendent Chris
Calabrese declined to comment on Shelton’s hiring.

There are significant repercussions when the state fails to take disciplinary
action. For one thing, it means that other schools receive no indication of a
problem. A red flag typically appears next to an educator’s name in a public
database when they are punished by the Commission on Teacher Credentialing.
But no such warning appears when a teacher is fired or forced to resign
without state discipline, leaving their potential future employers in the
dark. Nor would a confidential warning letter like the one Shelton received
result in a red flag. California lawmakers have tried to address the gap, but
[their efforts failed](https://www.propublica.org/article/california-teacher-
misconduct-database-bill-failed-al-muratsuchi).

Student victims, too, suffer long-lasting damage.

![A handwritten document in which a student says Shelton “hugs me when I
usually don’t want to be hugged” and sometimes “his hand goes to my waist.” It
says he also “placed his hand on my upper thigh,” making the student and a
friend “really uncomftarble.” “I see him get really close to the other girls
in my class too and makes me feel weirded out.”
](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/Shelton_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)A
handwritten statement from one of Shelton’s victims says he touched their
waist during hugs and put his hand on their upper thigh, making them
uncomfortable Obtained by KQED and ProPublica

One of the students who accused Shelton in Napa told KQED and ProPublica that
for years she wished she hadn’t reported him to anyone because she and her
classmates were characterized as liars after “we poured out so much.”

"It could've been stopped with us, but it wasn’t,” she said. “They didn’t
believe us.”

In Braff’s case, the Santa Paula Unified students who had accused him of abuse
continued to struggle in school as their former counselor kept getting new
jobs in education.

J. told KQED and ProPublica that for years she avoided acknowledging what
Braff did to her. "I couldn't place where all these emotions were coming from.
I was blaming everything else except the actual problem,” J. said, referring
to the abuse by Braff. “I didn't want to live anymore.”  

J., now a high school senior, has been homeschooled by her mother for almost
three years. She said she still has nightmares in which Braff yells at her for
“telling on him.”

And she has long faced doubts from others about her account of what happened
to her in elementary school. A few years ago, she recalled, a former classmate
told her: “Why would they let him go work somewhere else if he did that to
you?”
